title: Am I the only one who loves Kevin Costner as a director?

commenti.body: [removed]

I haven't watched too much of his directorial output. I do like Dances with Wolves, although perhaps less for its directing as such. Having said that, the Buffalo hunt sequence could hardly be improved upon: its a symphony of thundering hooves and as exciting as anything in any movie.

I haven't seen *Horizon* yet. I love *Dances With Wolves* and *Open Range.* He has a great talent with westerns. 

*The Postman,* however, is every bit the pile of burning garbage everyone felt it to be on release, and that falls on Costner's shoulders.
[removed]

Hubris and ego are palpable in his worst directorial efforts. There's a little bit of that in DWW, but it works in its favor. Open Range, on the other hand, is fucking great and I will die on that hill.
[removed]

I really like Horizon and Open Range. He is too arrogant - I don’t blame him, or any actor, for becoming that way. Nature of the job. 

But it translates into how he shoots. Too many glory/glam shots. He hurts the stories this way. 

But! He’s made some greats, and will hopefully get to make alllllll the Horizonssss
Horizon is much better than its rep. A couple set pieces there that are maybe the best in all of Westerns.
[removed]
Just curious what you mean by hubris and ego? Over long? Saviour complex? Lol. I love long movies a lot of times.

I'm dying for Horizon Chapter 2 news, Chapter 1 has some iffy sections, but there are some scenes that really impressed me, and I want to see what he cooked up for Part 2, and I hope he gets to do 3 and 4. The duel by the water trough might be one of my new favorite western moments.

My instant reaction is that I'd lump him in the same category as Clint Eastwood - perfectly good on technical/procedural level, but neither of them put anything forward that make me say *now that's a Costner/Eastwood film*. They don't really take any chances - they deliver competency, which is just as much a commendation of the team that surrounds them

Both, actually. Don't get me wrong, I do like long movies, even a few of Costner's, but in Waterworld and The Postman you can see it in full force. The saviour complex, particularly. Even if he wasn't the director in Waterworld we know he was the driving force behind it and back then he was an A-list star that basically could do everything he wanted and so he shaped the project to his will.

To me, the Postman was a post-apocalyptic western with huge ambition! I'm already a sucker for apocalyptic films, and i really appreciated the theme of hope/rebuilding of society, with the idea that human connection and communication, represented by the Postman, was a unique idea. I feel he sets a great atmosphere with his sweeping shots and grand ideas haha. Others may see it as ego. 

If you like his westerns, I think you'll probably like Horizon. People have complained about the 'disjointed' method of story-telling, by jumping around from character to character, but I can look at them as little short stories or vignettes based around the central theme of survival. It has the epic scale and scope of DWW and some great scenes that have still stuck with me.
People complained it was slow and sprawling, but that's one of the things i loved about it. The West \*was\* slow and sprawling. I thought it helped the atmosphere.
I think Kevin Costner's willingness to use slow, meditative story-telling is definitely a risk he takes, but it's not flashy or 'technically' great.
How low do you think he ranks on the list of Best Director-winning directors?

I feel this is a misreading of both directors. Unforgiven is one of the best directed movies to come out of Hollywood, imo. Cinematography that favors the story over athleticism is underrated. 

Neither do a ton of flashy camera movements, but both know how to put together an amazing shot.

1000%. It is told in a very unique way, which I think is off putting to some. But I thought it was brilliant. The very end was the only silliness - I was very confused why the story started moving so quickly ahahahh
I'm so hoping he gets to finish all four parts, it could turn into something epic on a much larger scale, kind of like an extended Western saga we don’t get to see much of anymore. Fingers crossed
Is the very end not just scenes from the next movie?  That was my assumption.
The scenes from the next movie! It just jumped right over! Some movies will throw a montage at the end to tell how the characters ended up, took me a while to figure that’s not what I was seeing

I can see what you mean. I really appreciated the scale and the *idea* behind *The Postman* and *Waterworld* more than the actual execution. And funny enough, I just realized today that Costner *didn't* direct *Waterworld*—he’s so synonymous with it that I always thought he did!

He's hit or miss for me, but Open Range in particular holds a place in my heart as one that my dad and I have rewatched so many times, and Horizon was fucking great.  Really hoping part two ends up getting a theatrical release, because the cinematography in part one was absolutely gorgeous and deserves to be seen on the big screen.
Yeah it was odd the way it was kind of just tacked on, but I don't suspect that that will be the only view we get of those events.
[removed]

Costner took over the editing room from the director on Waterworld.  I saw The Postman at a screening and had no idea how long it was. Couldn't leave because I drove a group of people who were spread out in theater. Had no idea how long it was and found it grating and goofy after about 45 mins....Just kept waiting for it to end...and waiting...The crushing boredom and pumped up unearned hero worship still annoys me to this day. You know a movie is a piece of shit when the hero and villain meet up for their final battle and the villain says "Don't I know you?"

This is the tragedy of auteurism—cinephiles fetishize directors with flashy or distinctive styles while dismissing understated directors who don’t beat you over the head with their flair.

Oh ahahhaa you hit my third rail. I studied film theory in school - specifically, Marxism and feminism. 

The Auteur Theory is one of the big things that’s gone wrong in American cinema. It hides both the labor and the giant machine that make movies happen. Directors get blamed for studio choices; they also get all the credit (and a ton of money) for the work of potentially thousands. 

TÁR is so brilliant; one reason why is it takes this head-on. Starts with the credits. The Auteur is a fraud and a monster. Just hero shit from my guy Fields

Well I think he's dumber than a sack of shit for being a republican STILL and frankly, that's enough right now to not support him in any way. How you look at film as a medium at all or have the kind of career he's had and say "Yeah, I'm gonna vote for the big red R" means you can only have shit for brains.

Costner’s problem is ego. Most of the movies he’s directed (or been heavily I loved with)  are really good, but they are overly long. If he learned to trim the fat, more people would give his movies a chance (or if he turned them into mini series). 

I think He’s easy to hate because his acting. He can be pretty dull at times.
I absolutely love The Postman

There's just something missing from Open Range. I don't mind a movie that alternates dramatic tension with character development, but it happens too slowly AND it's not particularly good-looking. You tlak about "epic landscapes" and the "raw beauty of the frontier" but I don't see anything like that in Open Range. Even spaghetti Westerns filmed in Europe have a better use of landscape.

I love Dances With Wolves immensely. But I think the real beauty is in the script and maybe not necessarily Costner’s acting and directing. 

A) Anyone can make the Badlands look beautiful. We went there on a family vacation. My daughter made the landscape look stunning on an old iPhone SE. 

B) It sometimes has a 90s TNT miniseries feel to it vs an actual movie. It lacks the big sweeping feel of  similar neo westerns (Giant, The Big Country, The Searchers, Django Unchained). The one caveat is John Barry’s absolutely beautiful soundtrack. 

C) Costner isn’t a bad actor…but he’s certainly not a good one either. Dunbar is a very likable character but Costner just doesn’t have the skill as an actor to make Dunbar’s transition from John Dunbar to Dances With Wolves believable. Mary McDonnell (who really deserved to be a much bigger talent) did an excellent job and should’ve won an Oscar.

The story resonated with me. A young man unhappy in the southeast with a desire to see the west. I really loved it and I think that despite my criticisms it’s an excellent movie.
I admire The Postman simply for how daring it attempts to be and how much it falls flat. I remember when it came out how much of a flop it was and how people were making jokes about it.
He campaigned for Pete Buttigieg. I think he's converted to Democrat.
He also advocated heavily for Liz Cheney who is a pro-lifer more recently, so maybe he was converted to a republican again.

It's ambitious to be sure, but everything about it is three feet to the left of where it needed to be. Will Patton is a great actor, but as a post-apocalypse strongman? No. James Russo as Idaho? *Almost*, but no.

And the entire premise of people drawing hope because they believe the government has been restored... What could possibly be less inspiring?
Yeah it really misses its mark.
